It’s somewhat sobering to think that the Mafia franchise is nearly a quarter of a century old. Many of the people who make the games have been working on it for even longer. What began life in 2002 with the release of Illusion Softworks’ Mafia has become a significant franchise for publisher 2K. And, like most other series of similar vintage, Mafia has seen its ups and downs. But it is still alive and kicking, even now, 25 years later.

Today, August 14, 2K releases Mafia: The Omertà Collection, which includes Mafia: The Old Country Definitive Edition, Mafia: Definitive Edition, Mafia 2: Definitive Edition, and Mafia 3: Definitive Edition. There’s also a free update for Mafia: Definitive Edition on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S to add 60 frames-per-second gameplay — something fans have been crying out for for years. It’s a busy time indeed for the Mafia franchise and its developer, Hangar 13.

It is impossible to provide a comprehensive 'making of' the entire franchise and all its years of development in a single hour-long interview, but I gave it a good shot when I sat down to talk to Hangar 13 president Nick Baynes, Hangar 13 general manager Roman Hladík, Mafia: The Old Country game director Alex Cox, and cinematics director Tomas Hrebicek. Roman and Tomas, by the way, have worked on Mafia from the very beginning, joining the Czech Republic studio Illusion Softworks in the city of Brno to shape what would become the first Mafia video game. They’ve seen it all: the acquisition from 2K parent company Take-Two in 2008, the rebrand to 2K Czech, and the merger into 2K’s Hangar 13 in 2017, and they are still here, still making Mafia games.

So, if you’ve got even a passing interest in the Mafia games, I hope you find something interesting in the interview below. We discuss all the main games and the challenges they faced, get some insight into the decisions that were made at the time, and there’s even room for a little Mafia tease for the future.

Mafia 1

IGN: I think the obvious starting point is at the beginning, the initial premise of what Mafia was setting out to do. Is it possible to trace that line to where it is now and how it's evolved?

Roman Hladík: If I go back to the early times of Illusion Softworks, which was the indie studio where it all started, we joined it probably in 1998, if I remember well. It was at a time when the studio was already working on Hidden & Dangerous 1, the game, and the owner of the studio wanted to extend the business and basically establish another group. So he called a couple of us, but we were really young folks at the time with very little experience of making games as hobbies. And first we were thinking about something completely different, but then the owner of the studio went to an exhibition and came back with the idea or with the information that the game we were considering, many other similar games were being developed at the time.

We started to think about a game that would be about crime, police, maybe a policeman investigating the crime, but it flipped around later on. And I think it was Daniel Vávra who brought the idea that there would be a strong story, which was not that common at the time. And so it happened that the first original Mafia was mostly appreciated for the story, for combining the gameplay elements and the story.

I don't think that was a clear intention at the beginning. It just happened, how the ideas were coming together and what we liked to play and so on. So it was, I would say, pure passion at that time driving us to deliver something like that. And I have to say that we were all a little bit naive at the time. We didn't know what we were going to do. So we also struggled a lot to finish the game. It took us four, four-and-a-half years probably, and it was all right back then.

Tomas Hrebicek: I remember we liked the gangster movies, the romance behind it. So we were watching Godfather, Miller's Crossing, and Goodfellas. So I think that all combined also the idea and we were starting to talk about that kind of game and the story and enjoy the romantic part of the gangsters, but also to show the dark sides of it. And as Roman said, this time we want to bring this super strong story, but also it was the first time we started to do the cinematography in the games. I believe we were the first ones to pay so much attention to the cinematics part in that. So as Roman said, we were pretty young, naive, and we were learning. Myself, I was responsible for the cinematics, but I didn't have any school on that. I was just watching movies, analyzing them shot by shot. And all of us were just learning on the way and trying to do the best.

Roman Hladík: And it's fair to say that it was Tomas who brought the cinematic part to the game, and he does it still today basically on all the Mafias.

IGN: How did you feel coming off the back of the first Mafia? Did its success take anyone by surprise? Was there a feeling even then that this was going to be a long-running franchise and you had to start plotting things out in a grander sense?

Roman Hladík: I would say for us as developers, it came as a surprise. We didn't expect this original Mafia to be this successful. Maybe the owner, Petr Vochozka, at that time was hoping for a huge success. But I think to all of us who were on the team, it came as a surprise. Because finishing a game — and I think it's still the same — at some point it feels a little bit endless. You are still debugging and iterating on the game and we are already tired and frustrated. So I would say we had that negative feeling in ourselves.

But then when it came out and players appreciate it, it's always a pleasure to feel that feedback. If the game is well received, then you're getting the positive feedback. So definitely it was, at least for me, a surprise. And because it was a commercial success as well, it was quite obvious that we are going to do the second one.

Alex Cox: I started working on the franchise a couple of years after this was, but one thing that always struck me is how much of a cultural export Mafia was from the Czech Republic, at the time, a country that was still 10 years or so independent. And if we think about Tomb Raider and how that was for the UK as something that broke out as a video game property, I think that's double the case for Mafia from the Czech Republic, from a relatively small country in Central Europe, for the games being internationally successful was quite a big deal for you guys, I assume.

When I visited the country for the first time, I was very surprised at how many people knew Mafia when, for example, you're in a taxi and the taxi driver knows the franchise. It was much, much more high profile than I was expecting when I arrived there. So I don't know whether you guys enjoy any degree of celebrity in a way that might be surprising to people outside of Czech?

Tomas Hrebicek: I would say it took us by surprise because as Roman said, it took us so much time to develop the first game. I'm not happy with the output until I get the positive feedback from the audience. So I see a lot of things we can improve always. And also I would say the marketing was not back then, it was not that strong in America. And so it was a huge positive surprise how widely and internationally Mafia was known. So as Roman said, it was a commercial success, so that opened the door to Mafia 2. And I think Alex, you joined towards the end or the middle of Mafia 2?

Alex Cox: Around the middle, yes. I was working for 2K at the time and I joined the project when 2K were going to acquire Illusion. The game had been in development for several years with Illusion as an independent studio. Take-Two had worked with Illusion on many games before, including Hidden & Dangerous. And so there was a close commercial relationship between the studio and the publisher. And because 2K had a lot of faith in Mafia 2 in particular, the studio was acquired and Illusion became 2K Czech a couple of years before Mafia 2 was shipped. And that was when I first joined the story as a producer at the time at 2K.

Mafia 2

Roman Hladík: As Alex mentioned, it took us seven years to develop the second Mafia, which was even more than the first one. And why I think it happened? After the success of the original Mafia, we got a feeling that now we can do whatever we want. And the ambitions were really high. So I would say we set up the design and the ambitions for our second Mafia really high. And then obviously it was maybe a bit too big a challenge for the team to work it out. And also the technology has developed over the time. The competition was stronger and so on. So that was all the reasons why it took seven years. Well, again, we made it in the end, but it was also a long time and not easy time, all the time.

Alex Cox: But you mentioned the competition. It's interesting, isn't it? If we cast our minds back to that time, open world crime games were very popular. There were a lot of other franchises out there as well trying to do the same kind of thing. And there was a transition, wasn't there? Because the original Mafia was primarily a PC game. It was a game that was developed on PC. It had an awkward console port, but actually it gained a lot of its popularity within the PC audience because it was the first open-world crime game that was available on PC. Obviously had the cinematic approach you guys discussed.

But at the time, the big challenge, I think, was to move the game from its PC roots. We were in the pre-Steam era there. So PC was a relatively limited market. And there was a big commercial push to make the game into a console game to get out there alongside the other open-world crime games that were breaking out in the mass market.

And that was one of the big technological challenges, wasn't it? Because halfway through development, there was a big engine change, wasn't there? To go from RenderWare to start with and then onto your own engine, which contributes to the delays and create quite a lot of complexity and challenges there?

Roman Hladík: That's all correct. It was technology which was challenging, and it was also the growth of the studio, the team. Because when we were finishing Mafia 1, it was around maybe 30 people. But then on Mafia 2, we grew up to almost 200, if I remember well. So it was also about managing the bigger team and all the challenges which are coming with that.

Nick Baynes: At that time, I think I'm right in saying the entire team was in Czech?

Alex Cox: That's right. The whole team was in Czech. I mean, obviously the studio’s evolved over the course of time to be much more international, but there was a big culture change as well, wasn't there at that time as I remember. I was working for the publisher. We became very much more closely involved with development when Illusion joined the 2K group. And I think there was a big culture change for you guys there as well, wasn't there, in terms of how to adapt to something like a more modern game development studio.

Tomas Hrebicek: It was a great transition from this just closed Czech-only studio in Mafia 1, transitioned through Mafia 2, partially international because we have cooperation with 2K publishing. For example, all the motion capture for the first two games were happening purely in Czech Republic. And then the English performance was done by dubbing ADR post-pro.

During Mafia 2, we came already to sound booth studios together and we spent months recording voiceovers, playing the real dubbing of the cinematics. And the difference is really visible between the Mafia 1 and Mafia 2. So the cooperation was much closer. And then on Mafia 3, we worked with American actors in an American studio. So there was transition over the games.

Alex Cox: That's really interesting, isn't it? Because I remember the first game was translated from Czech, Daniel Vávra’s script in Czech, and then someone in the UK fixed up some typos and text issues in the script. In the second game, actually an American scriptwriter took the script, didn't they? And they spent months and months reworking it and actually working with the talent in the studio. So that was a big evolution in terms of the creative quality of the VO. And then obviously you guys were working to the VO when you were doing the mocap, so that was interesting.

And then by the time we got to three, of course, yeah, we were doing all of that creative production side of things had largely moved to America. So again, there was I'd say a step up in terms of certainly the Americanization aspect of it. It was quite unusual for you guys to be writing American games and stories set in America from Czech Republic, obviously, with a lot of references to TV shows and movies rather than lived experiences.

Tomas Hrebicek: What's funny, a lot of stuff in original Mafia 1 is from Brno, like the church and all that stuff. So we were just trying to get the American feeling from the photos from the books, but all the influences were taken in Brno, here around. On Mafia 2 and Mafia 3, we are able already to travel and take the pictures and real stuff in America.

IGN: How do you feel about Mafia 2 looking back, good and bad? Is there anything there that you think you could have perhaps done slightly differently?

Roman Hladík: Well, it's difficult to say. I have to say that I like the Mafia 2 a lot. Because I think we managed to get the atmosphere of an American city better than what we did in the first one, for the reasons which Tomas mentioned. Because no one of us was traveling to U.S. before. So with Mafia 2, we already had a chance and we tried to do our best to capture that in the game. It's always stylized. The city is much smaller than the real cities, whatever, but I think we got it in a much better way.

I think we've been criticized at the time that we are not using the open world as much as we should. That was maybe what was dragging our scores a little bit lower during the release. But it's interesting that over the time people appreciate Mafia 2 more and more. They don't see these flaws and they enjoyed the story, which is great. So I think there was a little bit of controversy in the Mafia 2 was released because it probably didn't match all the expectations from players, but it still delivered a very solid entertainment story and activities, which players started to like. I don't know how to say that. It's always about the expectations versus the reality, and there was a little bit of gap there. So I wish we could deliver more. But as we said before, it was a challenging project for all of us and we did our best, and that's what was released in the end.

So maybe if we do it these days, we would probably deliver more of the content to the open world. But that's all I can say probably.

Alex Cox: At the time, a lot of games were expanding outwards, weren't they? So I think what you say there Roman is completely true. What players expected and what they got was not quite the same thing, but it's not because of what we tried to — I think we were quite honest about what the game was when we launched it — but players quite reasonably had an expectation, I think, particularly in terms of more open-world content.

There were stories about we cut lots of stuff out of the game and things like that as well, which was swirling around after launch, which were quite exaggerated. I mean, to Roman’s point, it was a difficult game to launch and we did have to trim a bit of scope, but we didn't change the game dramatically from a huge open-world game to what it was. I mean, we are talking about a little bit of side content only really.

Looking back on it now, I completely agree with Roman. It's the game that came closest, I think, to matching everybody's fantasy in their mind about what they see when they see Mafia on a box. I might be repeating something that Daniel Vávra said in the past, that Mafia 2 was almost his revision of Mafia 1 almost to improve and resolve issues that he had with the first game and wanting to do better. And I think he succeeded there in terms of the story. And it hit that kind of Goodfellas kind of vibe, which resonated well in terms of the story, in terms of the tone, in terms of the setting and everything like that landed very well.

I just think it suffered a little bit from players' expectations at the time, when more was certainly considered better in almost every way for an open-world game. But yeah, I still think it's remembered very fondly, and I think for all of the right reasons, that's it’s lasted the test of time.

Roman Hladík: What I think worked well in Mafia 2 was this chemistry between the main character, Vito, and his fellow Joe Barbaro. That's probably something which people liked and it was really fun to see the story based on those two characters that works still today, I believe, when people play it.

Mafia 3

IGN: When it was decided that Mafia 3 would follow, what were you trying to achieve? It followed six years after Mafia 2, so there was a huge amount of development time there as well. It'd be great to get some insight into the ups and downs of that.

Alex Cox: Mafia 3 was a long journey, and actually that did coincide with another evolution of the studio structure as well. So my part of the story, I started working at the studio as a designer at that point so I can talk as a developer for Mafia 3. We started on a version of Mafia 3 in the Czech Republic. So there was a prototype version of Mafia 3, an earlier version of the game that ultimately we shipped, that we worked on for a couple of years after Mafia 2. And the goal was to go much more open world. So that was our whole angle on it. There was a story. Again, the story was quite a lot different than the one we ultimately shipped, but it did involve the New Orleans setting that we ultimately used for Mafia 3.

And again, it had quite a different design. We were going quite heavily into the idea of story optionality, story choices and things like that. There was a different hero. It was much more focused on the Italian Mafia kind of vibe, and it was more of a direct sequence to Mafia 2.

But that project for one reason or another fell on stony ground. We had some development challenges there, particularly on the technical side. Our ambition started to overreach because we were still basically building on top of the Mafia 2 engine, and our ambitions were starting to overreach what we were able to technically do, particularly in terms of — actually talk about quite straightforward development concerns — it was becoming harder and harder for us to recruit developers because the tech was so idiosyncratic. While a lot of the broad swathe of game development was moving to middleware and standardized editors and things like that in terms of how to develop, our internal technology was becoming increasingly difficult to recruit.

And also at the time, obviously 15 years ago, we were requiring people to move to the Czech Republic. It was more and more difficult for us to recruit internationally as well. And that was becoming a bigger need because we needed to bring in talent to help to meet modern expectations for open-world games. So we had various challenges there that ultimately resulted in a new studio being formed, and the studio being rebranded from 2K Czech to Hangar 13, the studio that shipped Mafia 3, and a new studio location being opened in California in Novato. And there was a reboot of the project at that point. We focused in on the New Orleans story part of the story from the first version of the game, but the reboot took a significantly different direction. And the new studio head who is no longer with us, Haden Blackman, who was also the creative leader of the project, took over.

And so that ultimately over the course of the next three or so years after that led to Mafia 3. So the same kind of design intent, to move Mafia more towards an open-world format. But the story changed significantly, about the civil rights storyline, Lincoln Clay as the hero, the idea of the black mafia versus the Italian mafia as the enemy. All of those concepts came in alongside a big shift in terms of the game design approach to, let's say, maximum open world, if we were going to describe it kindly.

Roman Hladík: I think that was the important change during the development, that the new creative mind behind the Mafia was Haden Blackman. But the studio, which at the time was formed at Novato, California, was not purely new people coming. It was also a lot of people moving from Czech to the U.S. who were then working from there. So it was a mixture of original Mafia developers and new people coming to California to work on Mafia 3.

Nick Baynes: And of course the team back in Czech continued to exist, so it was an extension of that team, right?

Alex Cox: Yes. And that was, again, another big culture change for the studio. The California studio brought in an awful lot of talent as well. We had the benefit of being able to recruit from places like LucasArts and others in the Bay Area. So that brought a lot of expertise onto the team, which was great.

Mafia 3 was another hard development. And unfortunately, I think our ambition, again, was ultimately what held the project back in the end. The superb story, all of the same strengths as the previous two titles. I think Haden and the narrative team did a great job in presenting this civil rights storyline, treading quite a tightrope there of putting that on the screen in a way that I think most games would shy away from. And so we're very proud of how that aspect of the project landed. It's just a bit of a shame that — I don't think there's any secret here to say that the open-world elements of the game actually ended up holding it back despite being something that we'd invested heavily in.

But the positive part of that story — the game did okay only, commercially, critically a little bit disappointing — but the engine, the technical aspect of the game, we did manage to solve, and our internal technology really got up to a great standard. And that actually in the end helped us to move onto the path we're on now, because that helped us to do Mafia: Definitive Edition and the remake of Mafia, which we did several years later off the back of the Mafia 3 technology. So there was a nice unexpected benefit to that once we did finish that game.

Roman Hladík: Something the team in California brought to Mafia, it was a little bit better set in the U.S. environment, I would say. We did Mafia in Europe, and it was always our stylized view of how the American cities are looking like, how the life is in those cities and how the American mafia works. So I think having Haden Blackman in charge and having so many designers in California, it allowed us to deliver more on what… I would say for U.S. market, it was suddenly not a European view of their country. It was more fitting the U.S. customers, I would say. That's what happened as well with Mafia 3. For the first time we used the likeness of the actors, which was not the case in previous Mafias.

IGN: Was the initial focus on open world a reaction to Mafia 2? Was it about the trends at the time? Why was that the big investment?

Roman Hladík: I think it was the feedback from 2. And to be honest, for us as developers, when you are building a huge city, you want to use it, you want to deliver other stories, other activities within that city. And what constrained us on 2 was our ability to deliver on time, I would say. So it was quite obvious that we are going to try in a better way in the Mafia 3. And I think it did well. Maybe the activities in the open-world of Mafia 3 might be a little bit repetitive, but I think you can spend much, much more time in that game and enjoy the environment than it was in previous Mafias. So yes, definitely the feedback from the players was the driver.

Alex Cox: We've got quite a fractured audience actually now. Each of the Mafia games is somewhat different to the others. There's maybe a consistent core through the middle of narrative-driven action adventure, but each iteration of the game has brought in a new tranche of players to our audience base. And actually there are a sizable number, maybe a more silent number of players that like Mafia 3, like that kind of, let's say, Ubisoft style territory control style open-world that we focused on in that game. And it was quite successful for them, particularly in terms of providing lots of gameplay hours. Everything that Roman just mentioned, that did land well with a sizable proportion of players. And actually of all of the games that we've shipped, Mafia 3 has reached the most players by far. It was the biggest Mafia game that we ever did in terms of its scope, its scale, budget, its marketing, everything, and was successful relative to all of those factors.

And it was, I think, a reaction to Mafia 2 by and large. Certainly because of where games were at the time, pushing more open-world was seen as the way to make the game better and more successful, certainly by everybody. There was a widespread belief that this would succeed.

IGN: People do compare Mafia to GTA, rightly and wrongly. You see videos comparing the two games all the time. Has the comparison to GTA become a part of the Mafia franchise, irrespective of whether you’ve gone more open world or linear? Is that a thing that has factored into any thinking around what you do? Or is it just one of those things that happens online and isn't really reflective of the reality of the audience that you've built for the franchise?

Nick Baynes: I think that genuinely at the studio, we've got our own path. It genuinely never ever comes up in conversation as a touchpoint or steering our strategy or anything like that. I think obviously there's a lot of stories about that game out there right now because something's coming out later this year! But yeah, genuinely, I think it's an internet thing. It's not something the studio looks at. So I think I'm afraid there's not a rich vein of answers to give you for that.

Mafia: Definitive Edition

IGN: The Old Country went back on that open-world investment again to a more focused, linear game. It’s been out for a year now. How do you feel about it, and what development challenges did you face?

Nick Baynes: Around 2018 is when I and Brighton enters the scene, so I'm the new boy of eight years compared to these guys. But I think it'd be remiss, I think, to go straight to The Old Country without acknowledging the importance of Mafia: Definitive Edition as well. Because I think that if you look at Hangar 13 as a studio, it had gone off in a slightly different direction around the time the Brighton studio started. We were working on another game, but the Brighton studio was growing. We wanted to ship something because the game we're working on ultimately didn't ship, but it was quite a large, ambitious game. So we wanted to ship something as a studio. We wanted to find something to help grow Brighton and build the teams and how we all worked together.

And we felt that it was an appropriate time to build on the Mafia 3 engine and do a remake of Mafia 1, which I think actually was probably one of the first wave of the modern remakes. I think now obviously there's a lot of ground up remakes that are made, but I think when we were doing Mafia: Definitive Edition, we were certainly one of the first ones I think came out of that. And that was interesting because firstly, it created this really great working relationship and team structure between the UK office and Czech, which is where the Mafia games are made pretty much exclusively these days. It also showed us actually the amount of love that came back for that game in terms of just the story focus, the rough size of it in terms of scope. And so when the studio did go through a few more changes a couple of years later and we were looking at what we wanted to do with the franchise, it felt like it was a good time to — you talked earlier about the through line — to go back to that almost to what made Mafia great in the first place. Very tight, focused, authentic narrative stories that really immersed the player. And for us, we were going into a new engine. We were going back to the origin of Mafia. It was very much a case of let's deliver a classic Mafia story and then grow it from there.

And by grow it from there, what I mean is also the additional content we worked on over the last year in terms of, when you add in the DLC and the extra free ride content and the open-world content that you can access there, suddenly it feels like a much deeper package. That was just to add that context in the middle of the jump from Mafia 3 to The Old Country.

Alex Cox: And I do think there's an interesting part of the story there because, coming back to what you were saying earlier on about the reaction to Mafia 2, well the reaction to Mafia 3 is also what's triggered this next part. So the reaction to Mafia 3 was questionable, of course, we've seen that in the reviews. And so the game that Nick alluded to was a reaction to that. It was a different game. It was a very different genre, but it was something that struggled to find its path internally. And over the course of several years was still in development when we decided to go back to Mafia and do what was effectively a side project at the time.

But actually, as it turned out, that other project never really found its path. But what did find its path was actually going back to the roots of Mafia and rediscovering something that, as Nick said, connected everybody in the studio. We knew what we were making. It was actually a game that by and large everybody in the studio wanted to make. It was playing to our strengths. We were learning a lot of lessons there in terms of trying to do a game in a different genre with mechanics and technology that we don't know how to do. It's much more challenging than maybe people anticipated. And finding a safe haven back in Mafia was great for us.

But then as we did the game — and that was actually very successful as well — and so when the other project faltered in the end and did result in some studio reorganization, we found a new north star in terms of designing back around Mafia. But also the principles that made the original Mafia and the remake successful — and it did do quite well critically and it did well commercially — was that linear storytelling mode. It still had its audience. The players of all of the previous Mafia games came back to it and they enjoyed playing it.

And so that set the scene really for The Old Country, because while The Old Country didn't increase in terms of scope or technical ambition, under the hood it was because actually we discarded the Mafia 3 engine and we moved to Unreal. And so, while on the screen the game looks smaller and more focused, actually a lot of development effort went into rebuilding the engine completely. So that's something that players don't see of course on the screen. And we were trying as far as possible to make it feel, look, and play like a next-gen Mafia title. But that kind of under the hood investment in having to basically rebuild the whole engine under the hood is what that game was partly about strategically in addition to moving the franchise forward in a new way.

Mafia: The Old Country

Nick Baynes: A couple of times during this conversation we've talked about maybe Mafia 2 not quite meeting players' expectations, or Mafia 3 maybe going in a way that some people liked, but other people felt it had stumbled in certain areas. I think that the franchise throughout from the very, very beginning, the fact that we've had such strong characters, such compelling stories and people fall in love with the worlds, I think this is why all of our games, the audience, the affection for the games grows over time. And I think it's like, even when there has been the odd mismatched expectation at release, you go on Reddit now and you see people debating which one's their favorite Mafia game, and you'll quite often get four different answers. There's a size book group that will say Mafia 3 is the best Mafia game. And a sizeable group will say Mafia 2 is the best match game.

The reason why it does stick with people and why it does grow over time is that people do love these stories and they do love the characters. And that was really one of the things we wanted to do with The Old Country. In fact, it was a very big thing for us at the start: the importance of finding a protagonist that players are going to really embrace and want to live with them and play the game in their shoes. And we certainly saw that with Enzo. I think Alex and the team did a great job with all the characters in The Old Country. The cast of characters is probably the strongest we've had in terms of number of strong characters that people have really fallen in love with. It's about playing to our strengths and making sure we're capturing all the ingredients of what really is the essence of Mafia.

Roman Hladík: It's interesting to see the reactions from the players. Because these days people are playing almost endless games with endless grind, they really appreciated a shorter, more intensive story. And obviously there are also people who want to stay within the world we've built and enjoy it a little bit more. And for them, we released the free ride and now the DLC. So I think it's also about the market developing somehow. And the appetite for huge games is also limited, and they might be missing the other segment which we are trying to get to.

Alex Cox: Looking back on the game now, I think there's a very warm reaction to those characters. And I think that, Roman, you mentioned earlier on Vito and Joe, Lincoln, this is the core of every successful narrative adventure game, isn't it? Ultimately, it does boil down to the story basics, things like the characters are what really sticks with players. We saw a lot of players come to Mafia for the first time with The Old Country and then go back and discover other games. So for people that haven't dipped their toe into all of the games that came before The Old County, this is a good opportunity for them to pick it up at that point.

I genuinely feel quite humbled and honored by the fact that we've still got so many people who've been there from the start, or some people who joined along the way. So we've spent all this time working on this franchise, working on telling these amazing stories. And we've obviously invested a lot in changing the engine and modernizing certain aspects of the way we make games with The Old Country. I'm not going to give you any details or talk about anything specifically about what's next, but I will say that we're very grateful that players perceived The Old Country so well, and it's given us the opportunity to continue to lead the way hopefully in telling these great narrative stories and keep on doing what we're doing. And so that's as much as you're going to get, I think!

items.title: Avatar Boat Ride Attraction at Disney California Adventure First Look | D23 2026
items.description: Disney has revealed a first look at one of the attractions coming to the Avatar Destination (colloquially referred to as Avatar Land until Disney gives us an official name) at Disney California Adventure in the form of a boat ride. This first look comes via a new rockwork model at the D23 fan event happening in Anaheim this weekend.
items.author: Ryan McCaffrey
items.content:
Disney has revealed a first look at one of the attractions coming to the Avatar Destination (colloquially referred to as Avatar Land until Disney gives us an official name) at Disney California Adventure in the form of a boat ride. This first look comes via a new rockwork model at the D23 fan event happening in Anaheim this weekend. Check out the model photos in the gallery below.

The model shows a ride system that will seem to have significant ride capacity, with the boats seating at least 30 guests each (for context, the Pirates of the Caribbean boats can fit 22-24 people). You can also see the Disneyland Monorail running adjacent to this ride, given that it will live in the northeast corner of the park, where Hollywood Land currently resides. Though the model certainly shares obvious similarities to the Na'vi River Journey at Disney Animal Kingdom, the ride vehicle is clearly different, as the boats at the Florida park only hold 6-8 people.

Speculation amongst Disney theme park fans is that this might share the same ride system used at the beloved Pirates of the Caribbean at Shanghai Disneyland, which, if you're not familiar, is vastly different from the classic Pirates attraction at the American Disney parks. That ride system allows for a lot more movement than just moving straight ahead. Perhaps Disney will share more details at the Disney Experiences panel at D23 this weekend.

items.description: In a totalitarian state, you play an observer who watches your neighbors in a strange city called Z. This is the premise behind The Watcher (aptly named!), which is in development for PC.
items.author: Ryan McCaffrey
items.content:
In a totalitarian state, you play an observer who watches your neighbors in a strange city called Z. This is the premise behind The Watcher (aptly named!), which is in development for PC. Check out the first trailer above and the first screenshots in the gallery below.

The developer, indie studio Yesterday's Sandwich, describes The Watcher like this: "The Watcher is a surveillance simulator set in a psychological thriller world. items.title: The X-Files Returns to Comics With New Series From Dynamite Entertainment
items.description: If you're jonesing for classic The X-Files adventures, you're in luck. Dynamite Entertainment has just revealed a new comic book series presenting previously unseen cases for Agents Mulder and Scully.
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
The X-Files franchise is suddenly heating up again in 2026. Fresh off the release of The X-Files: I Want to Believe - Vrach Frankensteyn and LEGO's very first X-Files set comes the news that Dynamite Entertainment will publish a new X-Files comic starting this winter.

What's more, the new series will feature a familiar face to X-Files readers. Dynamite's The X-Files series is written by Joe Harris, who previously penned The X-Files: Season 10 and Season 11 for IDW Publishing. Those books presented a different (and some fans might argue better) continuation of the classic TV series before Fox's revival seasons came along. The new book is illustrated by Riley Brown (Dead Acre: Black Badge).

Unlike Harris' previous X-Files comics, this new series looks to be set during the events of the original show, presenting previously unseen cases for Agents Mulder and Scully. Dynamite teases that more plot details will be revealed in the months to come.

“The X-Files has always been sacred to me," Harris said in a statement. "From my own early TV fandom on Friday and Sunday nights to getting to work on one of the greatest supernatural thriller/science fiction franchises in history, the further adventures of Agents Mulder and Scully have occupied a very special place in my head and career. I am beyond honored to write them and I am absolutely over the moon to work with Dynamite on this new series.”

The X-Files is the latest Disney-owned property to find a home at Dynamite rather than Marvel Comics, joining the likes of Buffy the Vampire Slayer/Angel, Gargoyles, and Darkwing Duck.

This new comic comes as fans continue to wait for further news on Ryan Coogler's X-Files reboot. Earlier this year, the series was given a pilot order by Hulu. The reboot will star Danielle Deadwyler and Himeh Patel, and it remains to be seen if Gillian Anderson or David Duchovny will reprise their roles.

Meanwhile, The X-Files creator Chris Carter is still hoping to continue his story and resolve Season 11's divisive finale.

Jesse is a mild-mannered staff writer for IGN. Allow him to lend a machete to your intellectual thicket by following @jschedeen on BlueSky.

items.title: Xbox Confirms Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Beta Will Feature Single-Player Campaign Mission for the First Time
items.description: Xbox is trying something new with the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 beta, as the company has announced this month's pre-release tests will include a single-player campaign mission for the first time.
items.author: Michael Cripe
items.content:
Xbox is trying something new with the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 beta, as the company has announced this month's pre-release tests will include a single-player campaign mission for the first time.

Activision's best-selling first-person shooter franchise is no stranger to beta tests. The series has long relied on similar testing methods to get early feedback (and push pre-orders) ahead of launch, but while every installment thus far has focused on multiplayer offerings, this year's Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 beta is changing things up with early access to a single-player campaign mission called "Entrenched."

Xbox CEO announced the move herself with an X/Twitter post, confirming that, in addition to a host of multiplayer modes and maps – including a new Zodiac Warzone Resurgence map – Entrenched will be available starting next week. She took things one step further by publishing a gameplay teaser for the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 story mission, which you can see below.

New exclusive single player campaign mission for COD MW4 Beta drops next week. Weekend 2 brings Zodiac, a new warzone resurgence map. Let's go pic.twitter.com/rYif62bFw4

— ASHA (@asha_shar) August 14, 2026

Where this sudden change in pre-release strategy is coming from remains to be seen. For those who like to stick to multiplayer, though, the beta will still have plenty to offer.

The Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 early access beta, which follows Call of Duty Next, will run from August 21 – 25. Its multiplayer maps include Rooftops, Silkworm, Transit 213, Cachette, Lotus, and Kill Block, with a variety of modes supported, too. This first weekend of play will be available for pre-order purchasers who locked in their copy on PC, PlayStation 5, or Xbox Series X | S.

The open beta will then follow from August 28 – September 1. While the Entrenched single-player mission will be available across both periods, the maps and modes will change between the two. The Lotus map, for example, will be dropped in favor of the Lithium map during the open beta weekend.

The open beta weekend will also feature the debut of that new Zodiac Warzone Resurgence map. Nintendo Switch 2 users will also be able to try out Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 during the open beta as well. You can see the full breakdown, as well as a first screenshot from the new Warzone map, below.

CONFIRMED. Playable in the Modern Warfare 4 Beta:

✅ Exclusive Campaign Mission
✅ New Call of Duty: Warzone Resurgence Map: Zodiac (Weekend 2) pic.twitter.com/WOXNGoUMw5

— Call of Duty (@CallofDuty) August 14, 2026

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 launches for PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X | S October 23, 2026. You can read more about the beta test here. You can also see how Xbox is reminding Game Pass subscribers about how to play day one.

items.title: Kingdom Hearts Is a Billion-Dollar Franchise, Disney Declares Ahead of Hotly Anticipated D23 Panel
items.description: Kingdom Hearts is one of nine billion-dollar franchises Disney has under its video game banner.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
Kingdom Hearts is one of nine billion-dollar franchises Disney has under its video game banner.

The news comes ahead of a hotly anticipated panel at D23, where Disney is expected to talk about Kingdom Hearts 4.

In a blog post, Disney said its Disney Games Group portfolio “spans nine billion-dollar franchises including Kingdom Hearts and Marvel Strike Force.” More than half of these billion-dollar franchises have come out in the last 12 years.

Disney games have driven an estimated $3.5 billion in consumer spend annually for the past four years — and crossed $4 billion this past fiscal year, Disney said. That includes all Marvel games, all Star Wars games, indeed all games based on any Disney IP, of which there are many.

Upcoming Disney games include Marvel’s Wolverine, from Insomniac, the Iron Man game from EA’s Motive, and Star Wars Eclipse from Quantic Dream, although there is a cloud hanging over the latter. Meanwhile, Disney is also the rights holder for Respawn’s Star Wars Jedi 3, Creative Assembly’s Alien: Isolation 2, and Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra.

Kingdom Hearts’ name on Disney's billion-dollar list perhaps comes as a surprise, given how few mainline entires have been released since Kingdom Hearts released in 2002 for the PlayStation 2. It suggests Kingdom Hearts games really do sell well, and goes some way to explaining the anticipation for Kingdom Hearts 4.

Speaking of which, a livestream of the ‘DEEP DIVE into KINGDOM HEARTS panel at D23’ will be available on August 15 at 4.30pm PT / 7.30pm ET / August 16 at 12.30am UK time. Disney said it will offer a “behind-the-scenes look at the making of the games,” but it’s who’s on the panel that has fans excited for what is now expected news on Kingdom Hearts 4.

The panel guests are Nana Gadd from Disney & Pixar Games, Tai Yasue from Square Enix, Haley Joel Osment, who voices Sora, David Gallagher, who voices Riku, and Renée Johnson, who is behind the Disney character voices. With a panel like that (Yasue is believed to be co-director of Kingdom Hearts 4), you’d like to think we’ll get something on the hotly anticipated sequel.

Kingdom Hearts 4 made a surprise appearance at the June 2026 Nintendo Direct to reveal a first look at gameplay years after the game itself was announced. In a separate post, Square Enix confirmed that Kingdom Hearts 4 will launch simultaneously for PC via Epic Games Store and Steam, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X and S, as well as Nintendo Switch 2.

"A new installment in the action role-playing series developed and published by Square Enix, Kingdom Hearts 4 gives fans a look at some of the characters that protagonist Sora will meet in the mysterious city of Quadratum," an official description for the game said. "Sora will once again journey to realms, where new figures cross his path and new powers awaken his next chapter. Kingdom Hearts 4 will be available at launch on Nintendo Switch 2."

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

items.title: Sony Wants to Create an Original Character IP to Rival Hello Kitty — and a Stressed-Out Insomniac Bear Is in the Running
items.description: Japanese character goods, like Hello Kitty, are popular worldwide for their cute and recognizable designs. Now, Sony is entering the fray. Sony Creative Products (SCP), the division that manages the Sony Group’s character IPs, wants to develop its own characters with universal appeal that can generate 10 billion yen (approx. $62.8 million) in annual sales by 2030.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
Japanese character goods, like Hello Kitty, are popular worldwide for their cute and recognizable designs. Now, Sony is entering the fray. Sony Creative Products (SCP), the division that manages the Sony Group’s character IPs, wants to develop its own characters with universal appeal that can generate 10 billion yen (approx. $62.8 million) in annual sales by 2030.

As reported by Nikkei, the aim is to create original characters that Sony can make merchandise and multimedia centered around. To this end, it has established a dedicated team tasked with creating potential hit characters, and even opened a special event space in Tokyo.

Living in Japan, you really can’t escape from mascot characters and their merchandise. Chances are your nearest bank, supermarket or fast food chain is doing some kind of collaboration with some recognizable bug-eyed cutie. Many companies, cities and prefectures have their own mascot characters (the best known is probably Kumamoto prefecture’s Kumamon). Then there’s the major player in character goods: Sanrio, home of the world-famous Hello Kitty and a whole stable of fluffy icons including Kuromi, Cinnamoroll, and Pompom Purin. There’s also San-X, the creator of Rirakuma, and the Sumikko Gurashi family of characters.

Now, Sony is aiming to take on this market with new original characters of its own. Currently in the running is Nemu the Night Owl Bear, who has racked up over 1 million followers in a year. Created in collaboration with Tokyo-based company Tsumupapa, Nemu is a bear character who worries so much about life’s problems that he struggles to sleep. According to a SCP executive officer Nikkei interviewed, this “stress-filled society theme is resonating across borders,” with the bear apparently gaining much popularity in South Korea. Further plans for merchandise and an anime featuring Nemu are currently in the works.

Sony’s goal of 10 billion yen in annual sales by 2030 for original IP characters is a comparatively high one. For context, a character in Japan is usually considered a hit if its merchandise racks up between 2~3 billion yen in annual sales, according to SCP. However, with the Sony Group’s broad reach across anime, music, game and film, an original mascot (or two) already has many potential avenues to score fans and generate revenue.

As for the video game sector, while Nintendo has Mario and Sega has Sonic, Sony has always struggled to find an enduring mascot. If you ask gamers who Sony’s mascot is, their answer will probably depend on which PlayStation generation they grew up with. They might say Crash Bandicoot, Sackboy, or Astrobot. Then there are the many human characters from one-time PlayStation exclusives that became associated with the brand (Lara Croft, Solid Snake, Kratos, Nathan Drake et al.). There’s also Toro Inoue, the white cat from the Doko Demo Issyo series who became a PlayStation mascot in Japan for a while. However, Toro lacks the widespread international recognition that Nintendo’s plumber and Sega’s blue hedgehog enjoy.

The current issue is that Sony suffers from a lack of fully-owned, recognizable original characters, and the SCP aims to address this. It has a track record in handling domestic events for popular character IPs owned by other companies, and for revitalizing specific IPs in Japan, like the Peanuts comic strip characters (Snoopy and co.), which it acquired in March 2026. SCP is also using technology to enhance peoples’ encounters with such characters at events.

To this end, Sony Creative Products opened the Yurakucho Museum in Tokyo. This space aims to provide immersive character-related exhibitions. Currently, SCP is using haptics to enhance a Pingu exhibition, including vibrating floors and gusts of wind. Sony holds the marketing rights to Pingu in Japan, and doubled the Swiss-born penguin character’s merchandise sales in the country last year (source: Mainichi).

But can Sony apply its marketing successes with well-known character IPs to its own brand new, original creations? Could we get tie-in anime series and games with some cute new Sony characters? Watch this space.

Image credit: Tsumupapa.

Verity Townsend is a Japan-based freelance writer who previously served as editor, contributor and translator for the game news site Automaton West. She has also written about Japanese culture and movies for various publications.

Then there’s the major player in character goods: Sanrio, home of the world-famous Hello Kitty and a whole stable of fluffy icons including Kuromi, Cinnamoroll, and Pompom Purin. There’s also San-X, the creator of Rirakuma, and the Sumikko Gurashi family of characters.

Now, Sony is aiming to take on this market with new original characters of its own. Currently in the running is Nemu the Night Owl Bear, who has racked up over 1 million followers in a year. Created in collaboration with Tokyo-based company Tsumupapa, Nemu is a bear character who worries so much about life’s problems that he struggles to sleep. According to a SCP executive officer Nikkei interviewed, this “stress-filled society theme is resonating across borders,” with the bear apparently gaining much popularity in South Korea. Further plans for merchandise and an anime featuring Nemu are currently in the works.

Sony’s goal of 10 billion yen in annual sales by 2030 for original IP characters is a comparatively high one. For context, a character in Japan is usually considered a hit if its merchandise racks up between 2~3 billion yen in annual sales, according to SCP. However, with the Sony Group’s broad reach across anime, music, game and film, an original mascot (or two) already has many potential avenues to score fans and generate revenue.

As for the video game sector, while Nintendo has Mario and Sega has Sonic, Sony has always struggled to find an enduring mascot. If you ask gamers who Sony’s mascot is, their answer will probably depend on which PlayStation generation they grew up with. They might say Crash Bandicoot, Sackboy, or Astrobot. Then there are the many human characters from one-time PlayStation exclusives that became associated with the brand (Lara Croft, Solid Snake, Kratos, Nathan Drake et al.). There’s also Toro Inoue, the white cat from the Doko Demo Issyo series who became a PlayStation mascot in Japan for a while. However, Toro lacks the widespread international recognition that Nintendo’s plumber and Sega’s blue hedgehog enjoy.

The current issue is that Sony suffers from a lack of fully-owned, recognizable original characters, and the SCP aims to address this. It has a track record in handling domestic events for popular character IPs owned by other companies, and for revitalizing specific IPs in Japan, like the Peanuts comic strip characters (Snoopy and co.), which it acquired in March 2026. SCP is also using technology to enhance peoples’ encounters with such characters at events.

To this end, Sony Creative Products opened the Yurakucho Museum in Tokyo. This space aims to provide immersive character-related exhibitions. Currently, SCP is using haptics to enhance a Pingu exhibition, including vibrating floors and gusts of wind. Sony holds the marketing rights to Pingu in Japan, and doubled the Swiss-born penguin character’s merchandise sales in the country last year (source: Mainichi).

But can Sony apply its marketing successes with well-known character IPs to its own brand new, original creations? Could we get tie-in anime series and games with some cute new Sony characters? Watch this space.

Verity Townsend is a Japan-based freelance writer who previously served as editor, contributor and translator for the game news site Automaton West. She has also written about Japanese culture and movies for various publications.

items.title: Project Revenant, a Unique Precision-Aiming 2D Sidescroller, Announces Public Playtest
items.description: Korea-based developer Mayfly is developing Project Revenant, a unique 2D sidescrolling action game for PC where you'll need to use your mouse to specifically target enemies in order to hit them. No spray-and-pray here!
items.author: Ryan McCaffrey
items.content:
Korea-based developer Mayfly is developing Project Revenant, a unique 2D sidescrolling action game for PC where you'll need to use your mouse to specifically target enemies in order to hit them. No spray-and-pray here! Watch the new trailer above and check out almost two dozen gameplay screenshots in the gallery below.

"This is not a game where you can spray bullets and hope for the best," the developers said. "To survive, you must master the unique combat system known as 'Precision Aiming,' where only enemies directly under your cursor will take damage. This is not a game where you can spray bullets and hope for the best. You’ll need to carefully analyze each enemy’s position and attack pattern, then strike with accuracy. Headshot an enemy to take them out instantly, shoot down a chandelier to crush enemies beneath it, or ignite an explosive barrel to wipe out a group of foes. Every encounter is a tactical decision."

Project Revenant promises unique gameplay twists on every stage, unique bosses, a wide variety of enemies such as cyborg ninjas, giant robots, and bounty hunters, and varied environments. Check it out for yourself in the playtest beginning on August 26 on Steam.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked, and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch. He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan.

items.title: The Lord of the Rings: War in the North Dev Warned Warner Bros. Not to Go Up Against Skyrim Back in 2011
items.description: The Lord of the Rings: War in the North developer "argued vociferously" not to go up against Skyrim, but he was "overruled."
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
Cast your mind back to November 2011, and two big fantasy games based on established IPs came out pretty much at the same time: Bethesda’s The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, which went on to sell over 65 million copies, and Snowblind Studios’ The Lord of the Rings: War in the North, which failed commercially.

In retrospect, it was perhaps unwise for publisher Warner Bros. to release The Lord of the Rings: War in the North in the same week as Skyrim, given the extreme hype Bethesda’s behemoth enjoyed ahead of launch. But that’s exactly what Warner Bros. did — despite, it seems, the advice not to do so that it received from at least one high-ranking developer it had on its books.

Christian Allen was the design director on the WB Games Seattle leadership team at the time, working on the likes of Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor, Mad Max, and F.E.A.R. 2: Reborn. He noticed this week’s surprise Aspyr-developed re-release of The Lord of the Rings: War in the North across PC and console, and it sparked something of a trip down memory lane.

In a series of tweets, Allen said that he tried to convince the powers that be at Warner Bros. to avoid Skyrim for obvious reasons, but he was “overruled.”

“Wow, this is cool,” he began. “15 years ago I argued vociferously not to release this up against Skyrim, as it wouldn't get a fair shake. I got overruled. Nice to see it get a proper release.”

Why did Warner Bros. make such an obviously risky decision here? Allen added some context: “Quarterly revenue motivations drive more decisions than people realize. It's a big challenge with stock-price driven organizations. Must be hard to be an exec and go, ‘Well, this game will do better if we hold it until March, but my bonus will take a 50% hit.’”

Allen went on to talk about the impact Skyrim had on the visibility of Snowblind’s game. “At the time it really seemed to get lost in the wash, and every review just compared it to Skyrim (as I predicted they would),” he said.

“I think it only got like one review the week it launched,” he continued. “IIRC there was hardly any marketing, either they wrote it off or thought hardcore LOTR fans would just know about it, somehow.”

Following the failure of The Lord of the Rings: War in the North, Snowblind was merged with Monolith Productions, which went on to release Gotham City Impostors, Guardians of Middle-earth, and the much-loved Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor and Middle-earth: Shadow of War.

Last year, Warner Bros. closed Monolith down, having canceled its Wonder Woman video game. Allen is now design director on Steam hit Project Zomboid.

items.title: [UPDATE] Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse's Christopher Miller Says Leaked Footage Is 'Unfinished' and 'Not Fully Rendered'
items.description: The hotly anticipated Spider-Man: Beyond The Spider-Verse has suffered a significant leak, with four minutes of footage hitting social media today.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
UPDATE: Writer and producer Christopher Miller has addressed the Spider-Man: Beyond The Spider-Verse leak in a post on social media.

"Not a fan of leaks of unfinished, not fully rendered footage," he said in a tweet.

The comment confirms the legitimacy of the footage, but also suggests it's not what fans can expect to see in the finished movie when it comes out next year. It is unclear how the footage made its way online.

ORIGINAL STORY: The hotly anticipated Spider-Man: Beyond The Spider-Verse has suffered a significant leak, with four minutes of footage hitting social media today.

Sony is currently battling to scrub the footage from the likes of X / Twitter, but it faces an uphill challenge as users share the clip across multiple social channels.

The footage, which appears to be from the opening of the animated movie, also includes a trailer montage that points to the current June 18, 2027 release date. It is thought this is the footage shown behind closed doors at CinemaCon earlier this year.

This is the latest video leak Sony and indeed Marvel have suffered in recent years, with everything from Tom Holland’s Spider-Man films to Avengers: Doomsday content leaking all over the internet.

Beyond The Spider-Verse, directed by Bob Persichetti and Justin K. Thompson, with a story written by Phil Lord, Christopher Miller, and David Callaham, is the final chapter of Sony Pictures Animation's Oscar-winning Spider-Verse saga. It follows 2018's Into the Spider-Verse and 2023's Across the Spider-Verse. If the animated movie hits its current release date, it’ll arrive four years after Across the Spider-Verse and eight years after Into the Spider-Verse came out.

Here’s the official description:

Hunted by Miguel O’Hara’s Spider Society and betrayed by his friends, Miles finds himself in the darkest corners of the Spider-Verse in search of a way home. Knowing that his family has been not only fractured but endangered by his calling, it’s a race against the clock for Miles to travel across the wildest reaches of time and space to fight for and reunite everything he holds most dear.

Speaking to Variety in March, Lord and Miller insisted Beyond the Spider-Verse was on track, calling the movie the “most emotional” film in the trilogy. “It’s on schedule and it’s going to be beautiful and emotional,” Lord said. “I would say the most emotional of the three,” Miller added. He went on to talk about the new ways Spot is being animated.

Warning! Spoilers for the Spider-Verse movies follow:

Dr. Johnathon Ohnn, aka the Spot, is the main antagonist of the Spider-Verse movies. The former Alchemax scientist was transformed into a portal-creating supervillain when Miles Morales destroyed Kingpin’s Super-Collider. Spot is really, really angry at Miles, who he blames for ruining his life. And at the end of Across the Spider-Verse, after becoming incredibly powerful, he sets out to murder Miles' father, Jefferson Davis.

Spot steals pretty much every scene he’s in, with his wonderfully animated portal power fuelling increasingly elaborate, mind-bending action scenes. “... there are some new things they’re developing for the look… of what Spot does specifically that are extra amazing,” Miller said, teasing even more Spot mayhem.

“They’re really extraordinary. They’re going to be great,” Lord said, adding: “... artistically… It’s going to take you to places of abstraction that I think are going to be really special.”

In February, Lord and Miller explained why Beyond the Spider-Verse was taking so long. They said that a lot of the delay had to do with the pressure they put on themselves to outdo the previous two movies, which enjoyed critical and commercial acclaim, and the sheer amount of work required to come up with something that would do just that. Then there were issues that came with the decision to split the sequel in two, and subsequently having to piece it back together to create not just a coherent trilogy, but coherent individual movies.

“At one point it was one movie, but there was too much movie there, so it was separated into two,” Miller told io9. “But then once you looked at that second half of a movie, you’re like, ‘Well, that’s like not just a story arc that has a beginning, middle, and end.”

“We know where it’s headed, but we need to understand better what’s happening in the middle,” Lord added. “And we came upon a really wonderful notion, which is when your family is broken apart by your calling, your talents, how do you put them back together? How do you have it all?”

“We put the most pressure on ourselves,” Miller went on to say. “There’s no one that puts more pressure on us than ourselves, wanting to outdo ourselves each time and see things that you haven’t seen before and make it feel like something you’ve never experienced before. And so, trying to get something that is as worthy as the previous two has been the driver.”

“Having to take it apart to put it back together again was really, really [the] real thing that made it take longer,” Miller said.

Daniel Kaluuya, who played Hobart "Hobie" Brown / Spider-Punk in Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, is set to play the same character in Beyond the Spider-Verse (he’s also set to reprise the role in a Spider-Punk animated spinoff). Marvin Jones III, who voices supervillain Tombstone in Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, is also set to reprise his role for Beyond the Spider-Verse.

items.title: The X-Files Creator Chris Carter Wants to Continue the Story on From the Divisive Season 11 Finale
items.description: IGN interviews Chris Carter on The X-Files: I Want to Believe - Vrach Frankenshteyn and finally continuing the mainline story.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
Chris Carter knows The X-Files isn’t finished. At least, the story isn’t finished. Some believe The X-Files finally came to an end on March 21, 2018, following its Season 11 finale. But that episode, My Struggle IV, ended on a reveal that, clearly, was meant to be explored further — even as it divided fans. The question is, will Chris Carter, who created the much-loved alien conspiracy thriller back in the early ‘90s, get the chance?

I interviewed Carter to talk about the release of The X-Files: I Want to Believe - Vrach Frankenshteyn, his Director’s Cut of the second X-Files movie. As a veteran X-Files fan, I appreciated the opportunity to return to the world of 1998 and Mulder and Scully doing monster of the week things for an hour-and-a-half. As our The X-Files: I Want to Believe - Vrach Frankenshteyn review says, this new, horror-leaning version of the movie won’t change anyone’s mind about it. But it certainly left me wondering about what’s next for Carter and his The X-Files.

So, what is next? Carter told me he has a “big reveal” for fans and really does want to make it a reality, but it sounds unclear if that will be via a new The X-Files TV series or a movie. Certainly nothing is greenlit. All the while, a new version of The X-Files is in the works. Sinners and Black Panther director Ryan Coogler has filmed a pilot for an The X-Files reboot for Hulu. Will that feature Mulder and Scully in some way? If it does, does that make it canon to Carter’s show?

For now, we have The X-Files: I Want to Believe - Vrach Frankenshteyn to fuss over, and Carter’s masterplan for his story to ponder. The interview in full is below.

IGN: I had watched the original version, I've watched your new version, and I'd love to pick your brains a little bit about some of the changes you've made and why you've made them.

Chris Carter: The reason I wanted to go back and do this is, when we made the movie and showed it to the studio for the first time, the executives kind of tore us a new one. They actually referred to it as torture porn, as if it were a Saw movie. They said, "This isn't a PG-13 movie that you promised to make for us." And they made us cut it back to what they believed was a PG-13 movie. And so we made that hurdle.

But the next hurdle was unexpected. Whoever the governing body is that makes the rules on ratings said, "This isn't a PG-13 movie," and we had to cut it back even further. And so I felt like we had to cut a lot of the things that I thought made it an X-File. And ironically, I could do more on an hour of television than I could do with this standards and practices, the censors, than I could do for a PG-13 movie. So I always felt the movie got cut back and didn't really meet the standards of a good, scary X-Files. That's basically the reason I wanted to do this.

IGN: And so what changes have you made and why have you made them?

Chris Carter: So it's funny, people say usually a Director's Cut, it's what's added back in, all the additional material. I've actually cut it back. And one of the reasons for that, I actually cut down on the Mulder and Scully, call it romantic line, because we had had two reboots in between, and I felt like people got a lot of Mulder and Scully romance in those two reboots. And so coming back to this movie, I wanted to cut that back and focus on the scary stuff.

IGN: What scary stuff did you want to add in?

Chris Carter: It's really more the Frankenstein story, which is why I've added this new title to it. I always felt like it wasn't appreciated as a Frankenstein story, and it's only nodded to at the end of the movie. The idea that came to me, the reason for this movie was I read about a doctor who had transplanted the head of a monkey onto another monkey. And I loved it. I thought that's X-File's territory right there. I actually sought this man out in Cleveland, Ohio. I flew out there and got to sit with him at Case Western University and talk to him about the actual surgery. It was successful. The monkey ended up dying, but it was a successful head transplant. And that really was the idea behind I Want to Believe.

I Want to Believe, actually, the title, which comes right from the X-Files series, really informed the movie and the storytelling. But even more so, the beating heart of the show was ‘Don't Give Up.’ And that came because of a... I had gone to a talk with a very smart, soulful man named Huston Smith, who's no longer with us. I went to a talk that he gave, and he's a religious scholar, and he just took us all over with his experiences, his learning, his beliefs. And so it was about an hour-and-a-half of him completely entrancing us. And at the end of his talk, somebody raised their hand and said, "If you could sum up your experiences and knowledge in a sentence, what would it be?" And I cringed. I thought, oh my gosh, this man has just imparted all of this wisdom, and this person's asking for the bumper sticker.

And he thought about it, kind of looked up to the stars, and looked back and said, "Don't give up." And I thought, that's it. That's the secret to life itself. And I had to put that in the movie because I felt that it is the secret. Now, it could also be something reduced to a Nike t-shirt, but I thought there was such wisdom in those three words.

IGN: In 2026, how relevant do you feel The X-Files is?

Chris Carter: I'm going to tell you, I think it is relevant because everyone keeps telling me it's relevant. There's a huge hardcore fanbase out there, and bless their hearts, they've adopted Mulder and Scully. I think it's really those two characters are the secret to our success. Their relationship wasn't just romantic. It's respectful. It is combative. It is, for me, my perfect idea of a romance, of a relationship, of a friendship, of a mutually respectful relationship. And I think that's simply the reason that people are still drawn to the show.

I think we told great stories. I think great people came to work on the show and made it better. And I was just visiting one of those people the other day, David Nutter, who came and directed some of our very best episodes. I'm working on something right now with Glen Morgan, who he and his partner, James Wong, wrote some of our best episodes and then directed some of them too. I'm still working with these people. Darin Morgan came in and wrote some of the funniest X-Files episodes ever. So it's not just good storytelling. It's not just Mulder and Scully. It is the inspiration that these people brought to the concept itself.

IGN: I know there's other X-Files things happening, but your story was clearly not finished based on the last season and how it ended with the pregnancy reveal. What's the plan?

Chris Carter: There were four episodes that I worked on, they were called My Struggle I, My Struggle II, III, and IV. And they were all a setup for where I imagined the series would go. I have a big reveal for everyone, and I'm excited to do that if we ever have another chance. Ryan Coogler is doing his version of The X-Files, and I don't want to do anything to spoil that, get in the way of that, affect that. So we'll give him that respect and that space that he deserves. But I do have something... I do have another story or a series or a movie in where I want to explore that storyline that I've set up so carefully.

The X-Files: I Want to Believe - Vrach Frankenshteyn premieres on Disney+ and Hulu on August 14, 2026.
